newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: CLAIMS AUSTRALIA RESPONSIBLE FOR GOLD PLUNGE REJECTED
Deputy Prime Minister, Tim Fischer, has rejected claims that the Australian Government is responsible for the plunge in world gold prices.
Instead, Mr Fischer has blamed what he calls "24 year-old screen jockeys with braces" in the world's financial markets for the current bullion price doldrums.
" They should accept more of the responsibility. If they've got to close out or hedge with pain, the speculative positions they've taken, I'm not going to shed one tear for them," he said.
Mr Fischer was speaking in South Africa, where 60 per cent of the country's mines have been rendered unprofitable by the recent fall.
He said the gold price is set by traders around world, and it is unfair to blame Canberra.
YACHTING LEGEND DIES AT THE AGE OF 82
One of Australia's greatest blue water legends, Jock Sturrock died yesterday at the age of 82.
He was an Olympian four times, skipper of our first Americas Cup challenge and a yachtsman of international renown.
Sturrock was Australia's first Olympic medallist and the first man to take an Americas Cup race off the Americans.
He was named the Australian of the Year in 1962 and the Australian Yachtsman of the year.
Sturrock is survived by his wife Lynne.
RED CENTRE RAIL LINK VITAL TO AUSTRALIA'S DEFENCE: BEAZLEY
The Federal Opposition Leader says construction of the Alice Springs to Darwin rail link is vital to Australia's defence interests.
Kim Beazley said the importance of the link was brought home to him during defence exercises in the Northern Territory three years ago.
He said the Stuart Highway was clogged by defence vehicles and a third of the supplies had to be sent by sea.
Mr Beazley said with the interest of a private consortium, the Federal Government could easily afford the project, even without the Federation Fund.
"In in the situation of a conflict if you actually mined the Torres Straits then you'd be in a position where you'd be really stuck, so there was absolute evidence provided then of what we needed".
Mr Beazley said the project would also provide support to the Whyalla steel industry for several years and make South Australia the national focus for land transport.
STUDENTS TO RETURN TO TASMANIAN SCHOOLS ON MONDAY
The strike by Tasmania's Government school cleaners is over, but most students are not expected back before Monday.
The dispute, which erupted earlier this week over job security, ended late last night after talks between the Miscellaneous Workers Union and the Government lasting nine hours.
Both sides issued a statement saying the negotiations had been held on the clear understanding that the Government has a policy of no sackings or forced redundancies.
The statement also said a study into school cleaning will continue and that the union will co-operate fully.
ENGLAND GEARED UP FOR RUGBY CLASH TOMORROW NIGHT
In Rugby Union, English Captain Phil De Glanville says the
Australian team will be out to restore pride when the two teams meet at the Sydney Football Stadium tomorrow night.
The Wallabies lost to New Zealand 30 points to 13 last weekend.
England expects Australia to lift for this match, and De Glanville says the forwards in particular would have been stung by criticism from coach Greg Smith.
The English players have vowed to closely mark Wallaby fly-half Tim Horan.
De Glanville believes Horan is playing out of position and should be at centre, but says he is still a dangerous at fly-half.
"I'm sure that if he gets any space and time he'll be looking to use it", he said.
ACTU TO DISCUSS HUNTER COAL STRIKE
The ACTU executive will meet in Sydney this morning to discuss the escalating strike at a Hunter Valley coal mine owned by Rio Tinto.
The strike is over a new enterprise agreement and individual contracts.
Arbitration between the CFMEU and Rio Tinto's subsidiary Coal and Allied failed again yesterday and will only resume next Wednesday.
The dispute worsened when the union confirmed it had sent letters to the company's customers and market analysts warning of an indefinite dispute.
Hunter Valley Number One mine general manager, Allan Davies, condemned the move.
But, he says the company is determined to move coal from the mine while re-assuring its Asian customers of a steady supply.
Union President John Maitland says striking miners are not backing away.
He says the union will be talking to the ACTU and its affiliates and the dispute has the potential to "go wider".
